extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, electoral reformers, students of political theory, and informed general readers interested in suffrage and representative government
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and practical rules for constructing a representative democracy and for deciding who should have voting rights, how votes/representation should be weighted, and what institutional features (e.g., minority representation) are required to keep democracy effective and progressive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of persons, not geographic units
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament must represent towns and counties, not human beings; localities are not entitled to separate rights apart from their inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the human beings who inhabit towns and counties have their proper share of representation, local feelings and interests are thereby represented; there is no need to preserve 'local character' as an independent constitutional object. The legislator should treat persons as the unit of representation rather than artificial geographic entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal (proportional) representation to include minorities (Hare's system)
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of personal representation (as proposed by Mr. Hare) would allow minorities scattered across constituencies to unite and return representatives proportioned to their numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits include: bringing instructed minorities into Parliament; incentivizing selection of the ablest men because small numerical strength can count; improving the quality of majority representatives through regular contact with more instructed minority members; and enabling minorities to influence policy as moral powers. The scheme is presented as almost a 'specific' remedy to the exclusion of capable minorities under local-majority systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure presence of leading minds in the assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative assemblies should include some of the first minds of the country so that their influence is felt in general deliberations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of even a few superior intellects will raise the quality of deliberation and decision-making, act as leaders (occasional 'Pericles'), and provide higher-grade guidance for the nation. Mechanisms (e.g., proportional personal representation) should be designed to 'positively insure' such presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide institutional Antagonism (organ of dissent)
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate function of a representative assembly is to supply a permanent organ for antagonism — a social support and rallying-point for dissentient opinions and threatened interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without such a countervailing organ rival powers are suppressed, leading to stagnation and decay. Representative mechanisms should therefore secure an organized, constitutionally-provided space for minority or countervailing influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid collective mediocrity by hearing instructed minorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural tendency of representative government is toward collective mediocrity; this must be countered by ensuring the instructed minority is heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If superior intellects are entirely outnumbered and unheard, deliberation deteriorates. Systems should be designed so that instructed minorities have organs in the representative body to prevent decline in overall intellectual quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal suffrage as a means of civic education and inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule, all persons of full age who desire the franchise ought to have their voice reckoned; political participation educates and cultivates intelligence across society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluding portions of the populace removes the incentive to attend to public affairs and turns them into permanent malcontents or spectators. The franchise is also a matter of personal justice when a person is liable to taxation, conscription, or laws that affect them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary literacy and arithmetic as admissibility conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is inadmissible that anyone should vote who cannot read, write, and perform the common operations of arithmetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple, public, and fixed tests can be used at registry (e.g., copy a sentence from an English book and perform a rule-of-three sum) to ensure basic competencies; after a few years this condition would exclude only those who care so little for the franchise that their vote would not meaningfully indicate political opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal basic education should precede universal enfranchisement
rubrics_metrics.description: Society must make elementary instruction (reading, writing, arithmetic) accessible to all before universal suffrage is fully implemented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If society neglects this duty, temporary hardships arise, but the priority is to secure universal teaching first, since power over the community should not be conferred on those without the means to exercise it intelligently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation should be coextensive with taxation (taxpayers elect tax-voters)
rubrics_metrics.description: The assembly that votes taxes (general or local) should be elected exclusively by those who pay something towards the taxes imposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voters who pay nothing have incentives to be lavish with other people's money. To reconcile universality with this principle, visible forms of taxation should reach the poorest (direct tax or capitation), or electors should be required to make a small annual payment or be rated to assessed taxes so every electors feels a financial stake in public expenditure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests and registration rules must be public, fixed, and honest
rubrics_metrics.description: When imposing simple competency tests (e.g., literacy/arithmetic), the test procedure should be governed by fixed rules and complete publicity to secure honest application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents partiality, chicanery, and fraud. Simplicity helps ensure only those utterly indifferent are excluded after initial years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receipt of poor relief should disqualify (temporary disqualification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Receiving parish relief should be a peremptory disqualification for the franchise, with a proposed term (e.g., five years previous to registry) during which the applicant must not have been a recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The justification is that those dependent on others for subsistence have abdicated equal claim to privileges; similar temporary disqualifications should apply to uncertificated bankrupts or those under insolvency until debts are paid or sufficient time has passed. Non-payment of taxes, when persistent and not inadvertent, should likewise disqualify while it lasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions for suffrage must be temporary and attainable
rubrics_metrics.description: Any disqualifications (e.g., for relief, insolvency, non-payment of taxes) should be conditions which all persons are able or ought to be able to fulfill and therefore are not permanent disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These conditions leave the suffrage accessible to all in normal human condition; the loss of franchise is temporary and reversible upon restoration of normal social standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base plural voting on property
rubrics_metrics.description: It is inadmissible, except as a temporary makeshift, that superiority of influence (plural votes) should be conferred in consideration of property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property is an imperfect test of merit, often odious, and linking voting power to pecuniary qualifications compromises justice and makes the system impracticable in the long run. Any weighting based on pecuniary circumstances is likely to be resisted and corrosive to democratic legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural votes may be justifiably assigned for demonstrable intellectual superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: The only justification for reckoning one person's opinion as equivalent to more than one is individual mental superiority, approximated by education, examinations, or reliable proxies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where trustworthy national education or examination exists, education could be tested directly. In its absence, the nature (and successful performance) of a person's occupation can serve as a proxy — employers, foremen, skilled trades, bankers, merchants, manufacturers, and members of liberal professions may warrant additional votes if their occupation is bona fide and practiced for a sufficient period (e.g., three years). Degrees or certificates from reliable institutions or examinations (e.g., university associate examinations open to all comers) can also ground plural voting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupation as proxy for competence, with durability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Occupation can be used as a practical test of political capacity: employers and those performing superior functions are on average more intelligent; allow multiple votes subject to perseverance in that occupation (e.g., three years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevent people adopting occupations nominally for votes, require that the occupation have been practiced successfully for a defined period. Liberal professions and graduates with verified education/examination should be admitted to plurality of votes when teaching and qualifications are real and certified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple, public fiscal connection between voting and tax liability
rubrics_metrics.description: To align incentives with responsibility, have a simple visible connection between paying taxes and voting rights — e.g., capitation tax, rating to assessed taxes, or small annual payment tied to public expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes voters feel the money they help spend is partly their own and motivates care over public expenditure. It also reconciles the democratic principle with the need that voters who determine taxes have a stake in them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid artificial contrivances to exclude classes; change requires public discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations of the suffrage that involve arbitrary or compulsory exclusion of classes are not the solution; unfamiliarity is the main obstacle to reform and must be overcome by time and proper public canvassing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms must be debated sufficiently to render unfamiliar forms intelligible; prejudices described as 'insurmountable' are often self-fulfilling if reformers accommodate them rather than challenge and educate the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting of votes must be assigned on grounds comprehensible to electors
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigning greater influence to some on the ground of greater capacity is legitimate only if it is done on grounds which ordinary people can understand and perceive as just.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People are less offended by recognizing superior qualification than by permanent exclusion; weighting should be based on reasonable, articulable criteria (education, occupation, examinations) rather than opaque or arbitrary tests.
